title: Stop doing twenty of the same question

source.citation: Rohrer, D., & Taylor, K. (2007). The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning. Instructional Science, 35(6), 481-498.
source.finding: Students who practised different types of maths problem mixed together scored lower during practice but much higher on a test one week later than students who practised one type at a time.
source.caveat: The evidence for mixing is strongest in maths, where choosing the right method is part of the problem. Results in other subjects are less consistent, and the script says so.

scenes.narration: Doing twenty of the same question in a row feels great. It teaches you less than you think.
By question five, you're on autopilot. There's nothing left to choose.
In 2007, two researchers had students mix the question types instead.
During practice, the mixers did worse. On a test a week later, they did much better.
In an exam, nobody tells you the method. Mixing makes you practise choosing.
One warning. This is mainly shown in maths.
Today, pick three maths topics, shuffle the questions, and do them in random order.
